```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      eval = torch::torch_is_installed())
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
library(torch)
```

An explanation answers: which node features and which edges made the model
predict this? graphlearnR implements gradient based, perturbation based, and
optimization based methods, plus two checks of explanation quality. All
methods take a trained `graph_fit` (or a model), a graph, and a target node;
leave `target = NULL` for a graph level model.

## A model to explain

```{r}
g <- split_nodes(dataset_karate(), seed = 1)
torch_manual_seed(1)
fit <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gcn", 34, 16, 2, dropout = 0), g,
                         "node_classification", epochs = 100, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit, g)
```

## Feature attributions

### Saliency

The gradient of the selected output with respect to the input features. By
default the output is the predicted class of the target node.

```{r}
sal <- explain_saliency(fit, g, target = 1)
sal
top <- order(-abs(sal$node_feature))[1:5]
arrayInd(top, dim(sal$node_feature))
```

With identity features, feature $j$ of node $i$ is "being node $i$", so the
largest saliencies point at the nodes whose identity most affects node 1's
prediction.

### Integrated gradients

Saliency is local. Integrated gradients (Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan 2017)
average gradients along the straight path from a baseline (zero by default)
to the input and multiply by the difference. The attributions then add up to
the change in output between baseline and input; graphlearnR reports the
remaining gap of the Riemann approximation.

```{r}
ig <- explain_integrated_gradients(fit, g, target = 1, steps = 64)
sum(ig$node_feature)
ig$completeness_gap
```

## Edge attributions

### Edge gradients

`explain_edges()` attaches a weight of one to every edge, takes the gradient
of the output with respect to those weights, and returns a table.

```{r}
eg <- explain_edges(fit, g, target = 1)
head(eg$edges[order(-abs(eg$edges$attribution)), ])
```

### Occlusion

`explain_occlusion()` removes each incoming edge of the target in turn and
records how much the output drops. It also masks each feature column. It is
slow for many edges but needs no gradients and is easy to interpret.

```{r}
oc <- explain_occlusion(fit, g, target = 1)
head(oc$edges[order(-oc$edges$attribution), ])
```

### GNNExplainer

`gnn_explainer()` (Ying et al. 2019) learns a soft mask over edges and
features that keeps the prediction while staying small and close to binary.
The trained model's weights are frozen during the optimization and restored
afterwards.

```{r}
gx <- gnn_explainer(fit, g, target = 1, epochs = 100, seed = 1)
head(gx$edges[order(-gx$edges$attribution), ])
range(gx$edges$attribution)
```

## Attention

For attention models, `attention_weights()` collects the coefficients of the
last forward pass of each attention layer. Attention is a model component,
not an explanation; high attention does not have to mean high influence.

```{r}
torch_manual_seed(2)
fit_gat <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gat", 34, 8, 2, heads = 2), g,
                             "node_classification", epochs = 50, seed = 1)
invisible(predict(fit_gat, g))
aw <- attention_weights(fit_gat)
length(aw)
head(aw[[1]])
```

## Is the explanation any good?

### Fidelity

`explanation_fidelity()` keeps or removes the `k` most important edges and
measures the change in the predicted probability (Yuan et al. 2022).
`fidelity_plus` is the drop when the important edges are removed (higher is
better); `fidelity_minus` is the drop when only they are kept (lower is
better).

```{r}
rbind(gradient = explanation_fidelity(fit, g, eg, k = 5),
      gnn_explainer = explanation_fidelity(fit, g, gx, k = 5))
```

### Stability

`explanation_stability()` perturbs the features with small noise, explains
again, and reports the rank correlation with the original explanation. A low
value means the explanation would change for inputs that are practically
the same.

```{r}
explanation_stability(fit, g, function(m, h) explain_edges(m, h, target = 1),
                      noise = 0.01, reps = 3, seed = 1)
```

## Caveats

* Gradient methods explain the model, not the data. Two models with the same
  accuracy can have very different explanations.
* With one hot identity features, feature attributions are about node
  identity; with real features, they are about feature values.
* Always check fidelity before you interpret an explanation, and compare
  against a random edge ranking.
